lessons.explanation: The loop's stopping rule is an iteration count, and that is the bug. Normal requests need 20 to 30 tool calls, so a cap of 10 cuts them off. The right rule is `stop_reason`: the loop continues while it is `tool_use` and finishes on `end_turn`, the normal finish. A cap stays only as a backstop for a run that goes wrong. The stem sets two requirements and the correct answer must meet both: protect against a runaway loop, and do not cut off normal work.

a.reasoning: The model signals when it has finished, so a run of 5 calls and a run of 30 calls both stop at the right moment. A cap of 60 sits well above the 20 to 30 calls normal work needs, so it never fires on healthy runs, yet it still catches the infinite-loop bug that caused the cap to be added. Both requirements in the stem are met.

b.reasoning: It fails both requirements in different ways. The text check can fire early, because the model can write that phrase in a status update while it still has tool calls to make. Dropping the cap removes the runaway-loop protection the stem says to keep. The text check also adds nothing, because `end_turn` already says the model is done.
b.tempting: It starts with `stop_reason`, which is right, and dropping the cap looks like the cure for the 18% of cut-off runs.

c.reasoning: It keeps the cap of 10, so the 18% of runs that need 20 to 30 calls would still be cut off, which fails the requirement not to cut off normal work. The stall rule adds a second problem: useful iterations such as a dataset lookup or a check of a figure add no new documents, so three in a row would end a healthy run. It is also homemade logic layered on a signal the API already gives.
c.tempting: It starts with `stop_reason` and calls the cap a safety net, which is the correct idea. The cap's number is what gives it away.

d.reasoning: The count is still the stopping rule, only bigger. A run that finishes after 5 calls keeps going to 40, and the first request that needs 45 calls is cut off again. Reading `stop_reason` only to log it throws away the signal that should decide when to stop.
d.tempting: A cap of 40 sits above the longest runs seen so far, so it looks safe. It is tuned to the past, not to the model's signal.

concept: An agentic loop sends the request and reads `stop_reason`. While it is `tool_use`, the loop runs the requested tools, appends the results to the conversation and sends again. `end_turn` is the normal finish, so the loop returns. The documented loop keeps calling the API while `stop_reason` is `tool_use` and returns otherwise.

Other stop reasons exist, such as `max_tokens` (output truncated), `pause_turn`, `refusal` and `model_context_window_exceeded`, so a response that is not `tool_use` is not always a clean finish and the others need their own handling. Agents commonly have a maximum number of iterations to keep control, which supports a cap as a safety net. The exam guide's anti-patterns are an iteration cap as the primary stopping rule, parsing natural language to end the loop and checking the assistant's text for completion.

lessons.explanation: Citations are lost when the findings are handed to the synthesis subagent, for two reasons. The handover is unstructured, so URLs and page numbers sit in prose and the subagent has to dig them out. And the subagent sees only the prompt it is given, so anything missing from that prompt does not exist for it. The fix has two halves: put the complete findings in the prompt, and pass them in a form where each claim's source is its own field.

a.reasoning: The subagent would redo work the other subagents already did, guessing which documents a sentence came from using only the prose it was given. It is slower and less reliable than carrying the source forward with each claim from the start.
a.tempting: It sounds like a cheap way to add citations, but it repairs the gap after the draft is written instead of at the handover.

b.reasoning: When each claim carries its own source URL, document title and page number as separate fields, citing becomes copying instead of digging through prose. This fixes how the source is carried, and it is one half of the fix.

c.reasoning: It hides the gap instead of closing it: about 15% of the claims would be deleted, not cited. The second pass has no more source data than the first, so it cannot add citations. Provenance has to travel with the findings.
c.tempting: It makes the output look compliant, and the word 'removes' is easy to read past.

d.reasoning: A subagent does not see the coordinator's conversation or the other subagents' work, so the complete findings have to be in its own prompt. This is the other half of the fix: one change says how to pass the findings, this one says what to pass and where.
d.tempting: The stem says the findings are already pasted, so this can look like a no-op. But paragraphs of prose are a summary that has already lost detail.

e.reasoning: The subagent starts fresh, so there is no earlier discussion for it to read. Pointing it at sources it never received makes things worse: it would leave citations out or invent them.
e.tempting: In one conversation with one model, a phrase like 'discussed above' works. The trap is carrying that habit over to subagents.

concept: A subagent started through the `Task` tool begins fresh: it does not see the parent's conversation, tool results or other subagents' output. The only thing the parent passes is the prompt string, so findings, file paths and decisions must be written into it. There is no shared memory, and only the subagent's final message comes back to the parent. Since Claude Code v2.1.63 the tool is named `Agent`; `Task` still works as an alias and is the name the exam uses.

When the subagent must cite its sources, how you pass the data matters as much as what you pass. Use a structured format that keeps content (the claim, the excerpt) separate from metadata (URL, title, page number), so the source cannot be lost between handoffs. Anthropic's research system also adds a separate citation step after synthesis; that is background here, not a fix for this stem.

lessons.explanation: The fixed plan decided in advance what to read, based on an assumption about how the code is laid out, and the assumption was wrong. Nothing found along the way could change the plan. This is an open-ended investigation: you do not know where the answer is. So the plan should come from looking at the codebase and change as findings arrive. The two fixes work together: map the structure first, then plan from that map and keep revising.

a.reasoning: A quick map with `Glob` and `Grep` shows the Python scoring module before 60 Java files are read. Starting from structure replaces the assumption in the fixed plan with what is actually in the codebase. It is one half of the fix.

b.reasoning: It adds one more fixed step and places it late, so the agent reads the Java callees first and reaches the scoring module last. The plan is still fixed in advance, so the next codebase will have another blind spot.
b.tempting: It patches exactly the gap the stem shows, which makes it look like the targeted fix.

c.reasoning: An adaptive plan lets what is found steer the next step, for example moving to the scoring module once the time is seen to go there. Together with the map it focuses effort on the high-impact areas, which a one-hour deadline needs.

d.reasoning: The problem is choosing what to read, not reading fast enough. Reading all 1.4 million lines in parallel is brute force, and merged notes from every directory bury the one module that matters. Parallel work suits independent pieces, not an investigation that follows clues.
d.tempting: The stem has a deadline, and parallel work sounds like speed. It never decides where to look, so it does not fix why the plan failed.

e.reasoning: General encouragement does not change the order of a fixed plan or tell the agent where to look first, so it would run exactly as before. Being exhaustive is also the wrong goal under a one-hour deadline.
e.tempting: It names the real blind spot, the other language, without changing how the plan is made.

concept: There are two ways to split a task into steps. Prompt chaining is a fixed sequence decided up front, which suits predictable work where you know every step, such as a pass over each file followed by a cross-file pass. Dynamic decomposition creates the next subtasks from what the last step found, which suits open-ended problems where the number of steps cannot be predicted or hard-coded.

For open-ended work the guide's pattern is: map the structure, find the high-impact areas, then make a prioritised plan that adapts as you learn. An agent has to observe its environment and adjust its approach from what it sees, and research agents do better starting with short, broad queries to see what is available, then narrowing. Performance hunts and 'why does it take so long' questions are open-ended.

lessons.rule: When you do not know where the answer is, map the structure first, rank by impact, and let each finding change the plan.

lessons.explanation: The four checks are known in advance and are the same on every pull request, in the same order. Letting Claude plan the review caused both symptoms: plans vary, so some runs skip the changelog, and the planning step adds cost a fixed chain doesn't have, with the adaptive review costing three times as much as the old script. Both come from planning a task that needs no planning. The fix removes the planning decision and runs a fixed prompt chain. This is the mirror image of an open-ended investigation, where a fixed plan fails.

a.reasoning: A fixed chain of four prompts gives every pull request exactly the four checks in order, so the changelog can never be skipped. No planning step runs, so its cost goes away. When the steps are known, a chain is predictable in both coverage and cost.

b.reasoning: A prompt instruction only nudges a planner whose output already varies, so some runs would still skip a check, and the planning step keeps adding cost a fixed chain doesn't have. A fixed chain removes the decision instead of asking the model to make it correctly.
b.tempting: Listing the four checks by name sounds like it closes the gap, but it is still an instruction to a variable planner.

c.reasoning: The chain is the right base, but letting the model add steps whenever it decides brings a planning decision back, with the extra cost the stem complains about, for a list of checks that never changes. Nothing in the stem asks for more checks.
c.tempting: It sounds like the best of both: a reliable chain plus flexibility. It adds a feature the stem never asked for, and that feature brings back the planning cost.

d.reasoning: Running small PRs' plans on a smaller model adds a layer that makes the planning cheaper but leaves it variable. Having the agent list its planned checks first is still the agent's own plan, so a run can leave out the changelog. The gap comes from planning a task that never changes, and the planning step adds cost a fixed chain doesn't have.
d.tempting: It attacks the cost complaint directly, but it adds a routing layer and keeps the planning.

concept: Ask one question first: do I know the steps before I start? If yes, such as the same checks in the same order every time, use a fixed prompt chain. Each call processes the previous output, with optional programmatic checks between steps, and Claude does better on one focused task than on many requirements at once. A chain is accurate, predictable and easy to test.

If no, such as debugging or exploring unknown code, use dynamic decomposition: the steps come from what each step finds. Agents are more flexible but have a lower completion rate and are harder to test, and the best advice is to start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when it clearly improves results. Using adaptive planning for fixed work adds cost and variation.

stemSignals.meaning: The adaptive review costs more, and part of that is the planning step a fixed chain doesn't have. The fix should remove planning, not make it cheaper.

No step where the model decides what the review should contain.
An answer that removes the cause instead of adding an instruction or a cheaper model.

It lets the model add steps, which puts the planning decision back in for a list that never changes.
It makes planning cheaper but keeps it, so the changelog can still be skipped.

lessons.rule: Known steps call for a fixed chain; an unknown path calls for mapping and adapting. Do not add flexibility a fixed task does not need.

lessons.explanation: The ban comes from a regulator, and the stem shows prompt text has already stopped helping: a third example and a bold warning cut the monthly count only from 3 to 2. Compliance wants zero. A rule that must always hold needs enforcement in code at a fixed point in the loop, before the call runs. A hook that runs before the notice tool and checks the flag blocks the call, sends the agent to the human path, and adds nothing to the 99% of notices that are allowed.

a.reasoning: Examples are a probabilistic nudge, and the stem shows they have already stopped working. A regulatory ban needs a guarantee, so more prompt text is the wrong layer. Examples suit gray-area judgment, not a legal prohibition.
a.tempting: Examples worked a little (3 to 2), so more of them feels like the natural next step.

b.reasoning: A hook that runs after the tool has already fired is too late: the notice has gone out and the rule is already broken. Voiding and alerting only report the breach. Blocking has to happen before the call.
b.tempting: It has the right trigger, the flag from the account lookup, and a good clean-up story. It runs at the wrong point.

c.reasoning: A hook that runs before the tool intercepts the call, so no notice can reach a register customer, and the block message sends the agent to the approved human path. The check is deterministic code, so it guarantees the rule, and the allowed notices are not slowed.

d.reasoning: The register flag is already available from the account lookup, so a predictive classifier adds a new component with its own error rate to settle something the data already settles. A classifier is worth it only when no explicit field exists.
d.tempting: A dedicated check sounds thorough, but it replaces a certain field with a guess.

concept: An instruction in a prompt or in CLAUDE.md is a request, not a guarantee: Claude usually follows it, but prompts alone have a non-zero failure rate. A hook is deterministic code that runs at a fixed point in the loop, so it can guarantee a behaviour. The exam guide favours hooks and gates over prompt instructions for rules that must always hold.

`PreToolUse` fires before a tool call and is the enforcement primitive: it can return a decision to deny the call, with a reason that Claude sees, and exit code 2 also blocks. `PostToolUse` fires after the tool already ran, so blocking there cannot stop the call or its side effects.

lessons.explanation: The approvers lose 8 minutes because the handoff says only that a credit needs approval. A good handoff compresses the case into structured facts for the next person: who the customer is, what is disputed, the root cause and the recommended action. The two answers that fit are the identifiers with the proposed amount, and the root cause with its supporting evidence. Together they say which case this is and why the credit is justified, in a few lines.

a.reasoning: Dumping the whole session recreates the 8-minute reading task the approvers already complain about. A handoff should compress the case into the few facts needed to decide. A transcript can be an attachment but cannot replace a summary.
a.tempting: It is complete, so nothing is missing, but completeness is exactly what the approvers are drowning in.

b.reasoning: These are the facts the approver is currently hunting for in the chat: the verified account, the disputed bill and the proposed credit. With them in the handoff the approver can open the right records straight away.

c.reasoning: A score gives the approver a number to trust without a reason, and it leaves out the account and bill details the approver needs. A decision should rest on stated evidence, not on how sure the model says it is.
c.tempting: A single number is short, which fits the need for a quick read.

d.reasoning: This is the same kind of generic message the approvers already complain about: it says nothing about the account, the cause or the amount, so the approver still has to dig for every fact. Urgency is not a substitute for case facts.

e.reasoning: The cause and its evidence tell the approver why a credit is justified without re-reading the chat. It complements the identifiers: one says which case this is, the other says why the proposed credit is right.

concept: When work passes from the agent to a person, the handoff should be a structured summary, not a raw dump or a one-line flag. The exam guide's examples of what it carries are the customer identifier, the root cause and the recommended actions.

Structure is what keeps it short enough to read at a glance: each field answers one question the next person would otherwise have to hunt for. In a 'select 2' question, write down each problem first and match one answer to each.

lessons.explanation: The agent resolves the first two items and forgets the third in 30% of multi-issue messages, while single-issue conversations are fine. That is a planning and attention problem, not a compliance rule: no money or regulation is at stake, and the team wants no new components. The exam guide's approach is to split a multi-concern request into distinct items, investigate each, and give one resolution. A line in the system prompt asking for exactly that is the smallest fix that targets the cause.

a.reasoning: Multi-issue messages are within the agent's reach, and the resolution target depends on handling them. Escalating all of them is premature and throws away what the agent can resolve. Escalation is for explicit human requests or policy gaps, not for message length.
a.tempting: Handing off feels safe, but it trades a 30% miss for a human on every multi-issue message.

b.reasoning: This builds enforcement machinery for a planning problem. The agent never sees the missing item, so a counter would block the reply without telling it what is missing. Neither money nor regulation is at stake, so code-level enforcement is not needed.
b.tempting: A counter sounds like a guarantee, and hooks are the usual answer to misses. Here nothing must be enforced.

This is a judgment and planning problem with nothing to enforce, so guidance in the system prompt is the smallest right fix.

When the need is judgment and nothing must be enforced, guidance in the system prompt is the right and simplest tool. Start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when it clearly improves results.
For a request that holds several concerns, the exam guide's skill is to split it into distinct items, investigate each, and give one resolution.

lessons.explanation: The two meter tools return different units and different status formats, and a prompt table has only cut the error rate from 11% to 8%. The reliable fix is a hook that runs after each tool call and rewrites what the model sees, so the model only ever reasons about one unit and plain-language statuses. Normalising both the unit and the status codes in code leaves nothing for the model to get wrong.

a.reasoning: The stem shows the prompt table was already tried and left an 8% error rate. More examples and a self-check keep the work probabilistic, so the result still depends on the model getting each conversion right.
a.tempting: It builds on what already helped a little, and a double-check sounds careful.

b.reasoning: A hook before the call acts on the outgoing arguments, but the mismatch is in what the tools send back. Rewriting arguments cannot change the numeric reading type or the unit the legacy tool returns. Normalisation belongs in the result path, after the call.
b.tempting: It also normalises something with a hook, but it runs on the wrong side of the call.

c.reasoning: A hook after the call can replace the tool result the model sees, so the model gets one unit and readable statuses from both tools. It is deterministic code, unlike the prompt table, which cut errors from 11% to only 8%.

d.reasoning: Converting only the units fixes half of the mismatch. The numeric reading types still depend on a prompt legend, which is where the model keeps calling bills estimated by mistake. Normalising both fields in code is what removes the error.
d.tempting: It uses the right hook, and it is close. The leftover legend in the prompt is the gap.

concept: `PostToolUse` fires after the tool ran and can replace what the model sees with `updatedToolOutput`, and it can add context with `additionalContext`. That makes it the place to normalise heterogeneous formats, such as Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 dates and numeric status codes, before the model processes them. Hooks are deterministic and prompts are probabilistic.

`PreToolUse` acts on the outgoing call instead: it can allow, deny or rewrite the input with `updatedInput`. Choose the hook point by where the problem is: arguments going out, or results coming back.

lessons.explanation: The loop ends as soon as a response has any text block. But a response can contain text and a tool request together, so text says nothing about whether the turn is over. The loop should read `stop_reason`: run the tools and continue while it is `tool_use`, and finish on `end_turn`.

a.reasoning: `stop_reason` tells the loop whether Claude is waiting for a tool result, whatever text accompanies the request. Continuing on `tool_use` and finishing on `end_turn` fixes the early exit for good.

b.reasoning: Reading `stop_reason` is right, but a fixed 6-iteration stop cuts conversations off at an arbitrary point, and a four-bill dispute needs more calls than that. A cap is a safety net against runaway loops, not the rule that ends a normal conversation.
b.tempting: It starts with the correct signal, and a cap sounds responsible.

A response can contain text and tool requests together, so the presence of text says nothing about whether the turn is over.

Start with the simplest solution that works and add complexity only when it clearly improves results. A prompt instruction is a request that Claude usually follows, while a hook is deterministic code; a hook earns its place when a rule must hold on every call, not when the right order depends on which items the customer raised.

stemSignals.meaning: Two items, and the plan is raised first. That rules out simply following the customer's order.

stemSignals.phrase: offers a $90-a-month plan and then applies a $60 outage credit
stemSignals.meaning: The credit changes the balance, so the items depend on each other.

stemSignals.phrase: Most payment-plan requests involve no credit at all, and those must stay quick
stemSignals.meaning: Rules out a gate that forces a credit step on every plan.

The dependency between items decides the order of the resolution.
No new machinery for a problem of how the reply is composed.

eliminate.reason: It follows the customer's order, and this customer asked for the plan first.
It blocks every plan that comes with no credit, which is most of them.
It escalates routine work the agent can resolve by planning its reply.

lessons.rule: Split a multi-concern request into items and investigate them in parallel, but write one resolution after all results return, especially when one item changes another.

Checking meter reads first helps disputes close faster, but it is not a written policy, and 60% of plan requests come from customers who accept their bill. A hook would force a read on all of them. The proportionate fix is guidance in the system prompt, scoped to disputes, because nothing here has to be guaranteed.

a.reasoning: It forces a meter read on the 60% of customers who accept their bill and only want to spread it, adding turns to the conversations it was meant to shorten. A blocking gate is right for a mandatory prerequisite, not for a practice that saves turns.
a.tempting: Every plan backed by data sounds rigorous, and hooks are often the right answer in this domain.

b.reasoning: It keeps the benefit, reads first when a bill is disputed, and leaves plan-only requests alone. A prompt instruction is a request that Claude usually follows, which is enough for a best-effort preference with no money or compliance rule behind it, and it costs nothing to maintain.

c.tempting: It looks like the best of both: a hard gate for disputes and no friction for plan-only requests.

concept: The guide favours deterministic enforcement, such as hooks and gates, for rules that must always hold, and proportionate, root-cause fixes over heavier ones. Start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when it clearly improves results.

A hook is deterministic code at a fixed point in the loop, so it can guarantee a behaviour. An instruction in the prompt is a request, not a guarantee, but Claude usually follows it. The question to ask is whether the behaviour must be guaranteed. A practice that saves turns does not, so the prompt is the right layer.

stemSignals.meaning: The ask is to judge a proposal, which may be the wrong layer.

Guidance scoped to the case it helps (disputes), not applied to every plan.
No new code to maintain for a preference.

A gate keyed on the model's own tag is no more certain than a prompt line, and adds code.

a.reasoning: The model already sees a reason and still repeats the number sometimes. Stronger wording, here or in the system prompt, is still a request that Claude usually follows, not a guarantee.
a.tempting: The reason text does look weak, and policy language often helps.

b.reasoning: A `PostToolUse` hook does run before the model processes the result, so timing is not the cause. And returning a block from `PreToolUse` on `get_account` would stop the whole account lookup before it runs, which the agent needs for every conversation.

A `decision: "block"` with a reason only adds that reason next to the result, and Claude still sees the original output. So a block decision is a message about the result, not a change to it.

The fix on the result path (`PostToolUse`), since the call itself is needed.

lessons.explanation: The gate was right but failed open. When the approvals lookup timed out, the hook threw an exception, and a hook that fails lets the action proceed by default, so 6 unapproved credits went through. A money rule needs the gate to fail closed in both ways it can fail: a known error the code catches, which should deny and send the agent to human approval, and an unexpected crash, which should be configured to block.

a.reasoning: Setting the hook to block on failure (`onFailure: "block"`) means a crash in the hook stops the credit instead of letting it through. It covers failures the code did not foresee. It complements catching the timeout: one closes the gap for unexpected crashes, the other handles the known error with a useful message.

b.reasoning: The model can't see whether the approvals service is down, so a prompt rule leaves the outcome to its guess. Whether an approval exists is a deterministic check, and it already lives in the hook.
b.tempting: It names the right condition, the approvals outage.

c.reasoning: Retrying until the service answers holds the customer through a 15-minute outage and may still fail. It keeps trying when the situation calls for a person: deny the credit and escalate to the approver path.
c.tempting: Retries are a normal response to a timeout.

d.reasoning: Allowing the credit and reviewing it later is fail-open: the money has already been applied before an approver looks, which is exactly the incident in the stem.
d.tempting: It keeps credits flowing and still gets an approver involved.

e.reasoning: Catching the failed lookup and denying the credit, with a reason that names `escalate_to_agent`, turns the outage into the normal human-approval path instead of a silent pass. Credits of $250 or less never call the approvals service, so they keep flowing during the outage.

concept: The exam guide's Task 1.5 includes hooks that intercept outgoing calls to enforce compliance, such as blocking refunds above a threshold, and hooks that block a policy-violating action and redirect to another workflow such as human escalation.

In the Agent SDK, if a hook itself fails, the action proceeds unless the hook is configured to block on failure (`onFailure: "block"`). A `PreToolUse` hook can return a `permissionDecision` of `deny` with a `permissionDecisionReason` that Claude sees, so the agent knows where to go next.
Put together: catch the errors you expect and deny with a reason, and configure the hook to block for the ones you don't.

stemSignals.phrase: for credits above $250 only, asks the approvals service
stemSignals.meaning: Small credits never depend on the service, so failing closed doesn't touch them.

stemSignals.phrase: the lookup timed out, the hook threw an exception
stemSignals.meaning: Two failure paths: a known error and a crash.

stemSignals.phrase: 6 unapproved credits of $300 to $700 were applied
stemSignals.meaning: The hook failed open, which is the default when a hook fails.

stemSignals.phrase: Credits of $250 or less must keep flowing during outages
stemSignals.meaning: Rules out any fix that pauses all credits.

lookFor: A deny, not an allow, when the check can't complete.
A reason that sends the agent to the human-approval path.
A configuration that blocks if the hook itself crashes.

eliminate.reason: The model can't see the outage; the check belongs in the hook.
It holds the customer through the outage instead of escalating to an approver.
It lets the money move first and reviews afterwards: fail-open.

lessons.rule: A compliance hook must fail closed: deny with a reason when its check can't complete, and configure it to block if the hook itself crashes.

lessons.explanation: Only the calls the hook rewrites fail, and they fail for a missing `account_id`. That points at what the hook returns. `updatedInput` replaces the whole input object; it does not merge into it. The hook returned an object with only `reason_code`, so the agent's own arguments, `account_id` and the amount among them, never reached the tool.

a.reasoning: `updatedInput` replaces the entire input, so the tool received `{"reason_code": "OUTAGE"}` and nothing else. Credits the hook leaves alone keep the agent's arguments, which is why only outage credits fail. The fix is to return the agent's full input with `reason_code` added.

b.reasoning: It would fit if the agent's outage calls had changed, but the stem says they look the same as before the hook. The rewrite replaces the input rather than merging into it, which is why only rewritten calls lose their fields.
b.tempting: Merging is how many people picture an input rewrite.

c.reasoning: A `PreToolUse` hook runs before the call, so its rewrite is exactly what the tool receives. The error also names `account_id`, not `reason_code`, which points to lost arguments rather than a missing new field.
c.tempting: It mentions the right field and a plausible timing slip.

d.reasoning: It assumes the tool sees the session's history. A tool works from the input object of its call, and `updatedInput` replaces that whole object. The agent's calls are unchanged and credits the hook leaves alone go through, so `account_id` travels in the agent's arguments and was dropped by the rewrite. Inherited context is the question to ask about a subagent, which gets no automatic inheritance and must be given its context in its prompt.
d.tempting: The failures do start with the hook, and lost context sounds like a real way for a rewritten call to lose its account.

concept: The exam guide's Task 1.5 covers hooks that intercept outgoing tool calls. A `PreToolUse` hook can rewrite a call with `updatedInput`, which replaces the whole input object.

So a hook that wants to add one field must return every original argument plus the new one. Returning only the new field silently drops the rest, and the tool rejects the call for whatever required field it checks first.

stemSignals.meaning: The hook's output holds one field only.

stemSignals.phrase: every outage credit fails with the tool error "missing account_id"

stemSignals.phrase: while credits for other reasons go through
stemSignals.meaning: Only calls the hook rewrites fail.

stemSignals.phrase: The agent's calls look the same as they did before the hook
stemSignals.meaning: Rules out causes in the agent's behaviour.

lookFor: A cause that explains why only rewritten calls fail.
A cause consistent with the exact error text.
Knowledge of what `updatedInput` does: replace, not merge.

eliminate.reason: Rewrites replace rather than merge, and the agent's calls are unchanged.
`PreToolUse` runs before the call, and the error is about `account_id`.
The tool works from its call's input, not the session's history; the hook's rewrite replaced that input.

lessons.rule: A `PreToolUse` hook's `updatedInput` replaces the whole tool input, so return every original argument together with any field you add.

lessons.explanation: The loop drops tool results in two ways. When Claude asks for four reads in one response, it answers only the first `tool_use` block, and when a read fails it sends nothing at all. The API requires one `tool_result` for each `tool_use` block in the next user message, so it rejects the next call. The documented loop answers every `tool_use` block with its own `tool_result`, matched by `tool_use_id`, and still returns a result for a failed tool, with the error and `is_error: true`.

a.reasoning: The model can request several tools in one response; asking it not to only works around a broken loop, can't be guaranteed, and turns one round of four reads into four rounds.
a.tempting: It would make the existing loop correct without touching code.

b.reasoning: Running every block is right, but one combined result under the first block's ID leaves three `tool_use` blocks unanswered, and Claude can't tell which read belongs to which bill. Each block needs its own result.
b.tempting: It runs every tool, so no read is lost.

c.reasoning: One failed read out of four leaves three good results and an error Claude can act on. Ending the conversation throws away the work and the customer's time.
c.tempting: It avoids answering from partial data.

d.reasoning: When a tool fails, its `tool_result` still goes back, with the error text and `is_error: true`, so Claude can react, for example by retrying that read or telling the customer. Without it the block goes unanswered, so the API rejects the next call and Claude never learns the read failed. This covers the failure case, while running every block instead of only the first covers answering all four requests.

e.reasoning: After the assistant's response is appended to the history, the next user message carries one `tool_result` per `tool_use` block, matched by `tool_use_id`. This fixes the cause, a loop that runs only the first block: Claude gets all four reads back in one round. What a failed read's result must contain is a separate rule.

concept: When Claude wants a client tool, the response has `stop_reason: "tool_use"` and one or more `tool_use` blocks. Your code runs each tool and sends back a `tool_result`. The assistant's response is appended to the history, then a user message with one `tool_result` per `tool_use` block, matched by `tool_use_id`.

When a tool fails, still return a `tool_result` for it, with the error text and `is_error: true`, so Claude can react. The exam guide's Task 1.1 skill is adding tool results to the context between iterations; the history keeps the full context, so Claude builds on earlier results when choosing its next step.

stemSignals.phrase: asks for `get_meter_reads` on all four bills in one response, with four `tool_use` blocks
stemSignals.meaning: Several tool requests in one response are normal; the loop must answer each.

stemSignals.phrase: The loop runs only the first block and returns its result
stemSignals.meaning: Three requests go unanswered.

stemSignals.phrase: when a read fails it sends nothing for that block
stemSignals.meaning: A failure must still produce a `tool_result`.

stemSignals.phrase: tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after
stemSignals.meaning: The API's error when a `tool_use` block gets no `tool_result`.

lookFor: One `tool_result` for every `tool_use` block, matched by `tool_use_id`.
Failures returned with `is_error: true`, not dropped.
Fixes in the loop's code, not in what the model is asked to do.

eliminate.reason: It works around the loop with a prompt and adds rounds.
One combined result leaves three `tool_use` blocks unanswered.
One failed read doesn't justify ending the conversation.

lessons.rule: Answer every `tool_use` block with its own `tool_result`, matched by `tool_use_id`, and return failures with `is_error: true` instead of dropping them.

lessons.explanation: The pipeline passes only each subagent's final message to the next, but every step depends on details the step before discovered: tariffs need read dates, and the resolution needs both. Each handoff loses something, and patching the summary format only moves the loss, as the stem shows. The fix is to keep the dependent investigation in one context and use subagents only for lookups that don't depend on earlier findings.

a.reasoning: Each new field fixes the last loss someone noticed: once estimated months were added, rate-change dates went missing. The next dispute will need a detail the format did not foresee. A fixed summary format suits a step whose output is predictable.
a.tempting: It is the same move that already fixed one gap, and output formats are a real lever for subagents.

b.reasoning: Subagent pipelines fail when each step depends on what the previous step discovered, so dependent steps belong in one context. There the read dates, the estimated months and the rate-change dates sit together, and the resolution can credit the right period. Nothing crosses a handoff, so nothing is lost there; subagents stay useful for lookups that don't depend on earlier findings.

c.reasoning: Forwarding the earlier final messages lets the resolution see the reads summary as well as the tariff one, but this patches what crosses the handoffs instead of removing them: the dependent work is still split across three contexts. Each forwarded message still holds only what its subagent chose to report, and the stem shows details dropped from a step's own summary, first the estimated months and then the rate-change dates. Forwarding them unchanged can't bring those back. Passing earlier results along a chain works when each step's output is predictable enough that its summary holds what later steps need.
c.tempting: It keeps the pipeline the team built and gives the last step more of the earlier findings.

d.reasoning: A checker re-reads the meter and tariff data, which repeats the work and raises the cost per dispute, and the cause, detail lost between steps, remains.
d.tempting: An independent final check sounds like good practice for money decisions.

concept: The exam guide's Task 1.6 contrasts fixed sequential pipelines with dynamic decomposition based on intermediate findings. Subagent pipelines fail when each step depends on what the previous step discovered, because information is lost at each handoff. Subagents suit research and exploration where you need a result rather than the journey.

Only the subagent's final message comes back to the parent, and a subagent starts fresh with only the prompt it is given. So a chain of subagents carries forward only what each final message happens to include.

stemSignals.meaning: Information crosses each step only through a final message; no subagent sees another's working history.

stemSignals.phrase: The tariff step needs the read dates, and the resolution needs both
stemSignals.meaning: Each step depends on what the step before discovered.

stemSignals.phrase: The team already added estimated months to the reads summary, but now the rate-change dates get lost instead
stemSignals.meaning: Patching the format moves the loss; it doesn't stop it. The dates are dropped from a step's own summary, so forwarding summaries further along can't recover them.

stemSignals.phrase: Cost per dispute must stay flat
stemSignals.meaning: Rules out adding a checking subagent that repeats the reads and tariff work.

lookFor: Dependent steps kept in one context.
Subagents kept for independent lookups where only the result matters.
A fix that removes the handoffs rather than patching what crosses them.

eliminate.reason: Adding fields only fixes the last loss someone noticed.
It patches what crosses the handoffs instead of removing them; each forwarded message still lacks whatever its subagent dropped, such as the rate-change dates.
A checker raises the cost and leaves the cause in place.

lessons.rule: Keep investigation steps that depend on each other's findings in one context; pipeline subagents lose details at each handoff.

lessons.explanation: Resuming depends on session history that lives on one host, and the hosts are replaced every night while cases stay open for a week. So `resume` fails for most returns, and the agent repeats about 20 tool calls. To carry work across hosts, capture the results as application state and pass them into a fresh session's prompt. a.tempting: It never answers from old results, which sounds safe.

stemSignals.meaning: `resume` and forks both need that history.

The nightly deploy replaces the host, so most returns still find no history.

lessons.explanation: Every subagent covered what it was given: thorough sections with over 40 sources each, and synthesis used everything it received. The logs rule out failed calls, and a silent empty result could hide only data that was requested; nobody requested the missing sectors. The gap is in what was asked: the coordinator split an economy-wide question into two sectors. This is the overly narrow decomposition the exam guide warns about, and its sample answer puts the root cause in the coordinator's decomposition, not in the subagents. So the change belongs there too: divide the whole economy into parts before delegating, rather than widening one subagent's search, adding retries or allowing a longer briefing.

a.reasoning: The literature subagent was asked about one sector and covered it with over 40 sources. It was never asked about the rest of the economy. A subagent works to the scope it is given; widening the scope is the coordinator's job, so broader queries stretch one subagent while the split still leaves the other sectors unassigned. Broader queries would be the fix if the assigned sector itself were thinly covered.
a.tempting: Thin coverage often does come from narrow search queries, and broadening them is a quick change.

b.reasoning: A timeout that comes back as an empty success would also log as a success, so the logs alone can't rule this out. What rules it out is the assignment: the dataset subagent was given one sector, so it never asked for manufacturing or services tables, and a silent timeout can hide only data that was asked for. Retries and an error rule patch the retrieval step and leave the split that never assigned those sectors; they would be the fix if those sectors had been assigned and came back empty.

The coordinator owns decomposition, so a split narrower than the question leaves gaps no subagent can fill. The fix is to divide the whole economy before delegating.

d.tempting: Briefings for ministers are short, so compression sounds likely and a longer limit sounds like a simple fix.

concept: The exam guide lists the risk of overly narrow task decomposition leading to incomplete coverage of broad research topics. Its sample question has a coordinator split a broad topic too narrowly, and the answer places the root cause in the coordinator's decomposition rather than in the subagents.

Anthropic's research system found the same in practice: each subagent needs an objective, an output format and clear task boundaries, and vague delegation produced gaps and duplicated work. Getting the split right is the coordinator's job.

lessons.explanation: Two forks ran in one checkout, and one fork's tests failed on code it never wrote. Forking branches the conversation, not the filesystem: each fork gets its own copy of the history, but a fork's file edits are real and land in whatever files it is working on. Both forks edited the same working tree, so each design needs its own copy of the files.

a.reasoning: The cause is shared files, not shared conversation. Each design needs its own checkout of the code. Claude Code's docs run parallel sessions in git worktrees for this reason: each worktree is a separate checkout on its own branch, so one design's edits don't collide with the other's and each is built and tested on its own files. Running `claude --resume cache-baseline --fork-session` from each worktree still forks the same baseline into that worktree.

b.reasoning: Each fork gets its own copy of the conversation and the original stays unchanged, so the Redis fork never saw the Caffeine plan. A fresh session would also throw away the 2-hour baseline and still share the checkout.
b.tempting: Shared history between forks is a common misunderstanding of what forking does.

c.reasoning: The CLI flag gives a new session ID with a copy of the history, and the SDK option creates a new session with a copy of the history. Neither copies files, because sessions don't hold the filesystem.
c.tempting: It uses the exact names of the real flag and option.

d.reasoning: Running one fork after the other removes the overlap in time but not the cause: the Caffeine fork's edits stay in the repository, so the Redis fork starts on modified files.
d.tempting: Two processes writing at once looks like the obvious race.

concept: The exam guide's Task 1.7 includes using `fork_session` to create parallel exploration branches, for example to compare refactoring approaches.

In the SDK, `forkSession` (`fork_session`) with `resume` creates a new session with a copy of the history, leaving the original unchanged. On the CLI, `--fork-session` with `--resume` or `--continue` gives a new session ID instead of reusing the original. Forking branches the conversation, not the filesystem: a fork's file edits are real, so parallel forks that edit code each need their own copy of the files. Claude Code's common-workflows page runs parallel sessions in git worktrees so that their edits don't collide. Each git worktree is a separate checkout on its own branch, created from an existing commit, and starting another worktree under a different name in a second terminal gives an isolated parallel session. Resuming by name works across a repository's worktrees, and a forked session starts in the directory Claude is launched from, leaving the original session's worktree untouched, so running `claude --resume cache-baseline --fork-session` from each worktree forks the 2-hour baseline into that worktree.

stemSignals.meaning: Two forks of one baseline, running side by side.

stemSignals.meaning: One set of files for two forks.

stemSignals.meaning: Another fork's edits are in the files.

stemSignals.phrase: The Caffeine fork finishes first
stemSignals.meaning: Rules out timing alone as the cause.

lookFor: A cause in the filesystem, not in the conversation.
A separate checkout for each fork, such as a git worktree.

eliminate.reason: Forks don't share history, and a fresh session still shares the checkout.
Neither the flag nor the SDK option isolates files.
Running in sequence leaves the first fork's edits in place.

lessons.rule: Forking a session branches the conversation, not the files; parallel forks that edit code each need their own working copy.

lessons.explanation: The loop sends each round of tool output with a text reminder after the `tool_result` blocks. The stop-reasons guide warns against exactly this: a text block after tool results in the same user message can cause an empty `end_turn` response. The iteration cap was raised and nothing changed, because the loop is ending on a real stop signal. The fix is to send the results without that text block and move the standing reminder into the system prompt.

a.reasoning: Deciding whether to continue from what the text contains is natural-language termination, and it would loop on responses with nothing to act on. The empty response has a cause in how the loop builds its messages.
a.tempting: An empty answer does look like the model gave up too early.

b.reasoning: Nothing in the stem points to length, and trimming throws away output the agent may need while keeping the text block that causes the problem.
b.tempting: Long tool output can cause problems in long investigations.

c.reasoning: An iteration count as the stopping rule is an anti-pattern, and the stem shows the cap isn't the issue: raising it to 60 changed nothing. `end_turn` should end the loop; the question is why it arrives empty.
c.tempting: It treats the loop ending as the problem, which is what the user sees.

d.reasoning: User text right after every tool result sets a pattern, and Claude ends its turn to follow it; that is the documented cause of the empty `end_turn`. Sending the `tool_result` blocks without that text block removes the pattern. The Messages API reference describes the system prompt as a way to give Claude context and instructions, so "cite file paths and line numbers" can go there and is kept.

concept: The agentic loop sends the request, checks `stop_reason`, runs the requested tools, and adds the results to the conversation for the next iteration. The assistant's response is appended to the history, then a user message with the `tool_result` blocks.

The stop-reasons guide adds a detail about that user message: don't put a text block after the `tool_result` blocks, because it can cause an empty `end_turn`: user text after every tool result sets a pattern, and Claude ends its turn to follow it. A standing instruction can go in the system prompt, which the API reference describes as a way of providing context and instructions to Claude. Agents commonly keep a maximum number of iterations as a safety net, but the exam guide's anti-pattern is a cap used as the primary stopping rule.

stemSignals.meaning: The message shape the docs warn against.

stemSignals.meaning: The documented symptom of that shape.

stemSignals.meaning: The cap is not the cause.

stemSignals.phrase: "Reminder: cite file paths and line numbers."
stemSignals.meaning: A standing instruction, which can go in the system prompt instead of each tool round.

lookFor: A cause that matches the exact symptom: empty `end_turn` after a tool round.
Tool results sent on their own.
Standing instructions in the system prompt.

eliminate.reason: It decides on text content, the natural-language termination anti-pattern.
Nothing points to length, and the text block stays.
A cap as the stopping rule is an anti-pattern, and raising it changed nothing.

lessons.rule: Send `tool_result` blocks without trailing text; put standing instructions in the system prompt instead of each tool-result message.

lessons.explanation: The subagent wastes time at both ends: it starts from vague delegations such as "explain routing" and has to guess the module and question, and it has no defined output, so it writes long narratives that the main session re-reads. Both fixes live in the subagent's definition: a description that tells the main session what to pass, and a prompt that defines the output format.

a.reasoning: A subagent's description sits in the main agent's system prompt and guides the prompt the main agent writes for it. Saying "pass the module path and the engineer's exact question" makes delegations specific, so the subagent stops spending its run guessing. It fixes the input; the output format fixes the result.

b.reasoning: A turn cap ends runs on time but cuts them off wherever they are, so answers lose accuracy, which the engineers ruled out. The subagent needs a clear task and a clear finish, not a cut-off.
b.tempting: It directly targets the 10-minute goal.

c.reasoning: Only the subagent's final message comes back to the main session; its intermediate messages stay in its own context. Even if the main session could read them, the runs would still take 25 minutes, because the vague delegations that make the subagent guess would be unchanged.
c.tempting: Picking class names out of shorter messages sounds faster than reading the narrative.

d.reasoning: Switching models changes neither cause in the stem: the delegations still don't say which module or question is meant, and there is still no defined output to give the run a stopping point, so runs stay long and end in narratives. Neither problem is about the model's ability.
d.tempting: A stronger model often writes better explanations, so the model looks like the weak part.

e.reasoning: A defined output format is the most important improvement to a subagent: it gives a natural stopping point, so the run ends when the format is filled. The main session gets class names and files directly instead of re-reading 3,000 words.

concept: The exam guide's Task 1.3 covers `AgentDefinition` configuration: description, system prompt and tool restrictions per subagent type. In the SDK, `description` and `prompt` are the required fields.

A subagent's description is in the main agent's system prompt and decides when it is launched; it also guides the prompt the main agent writes for it. The most important improvement to a subagent is a defined output format, which gives a natural stopping point and stops it running too long.
The prompt string is the only thing passed from the parent, and only the final message comes back, so both ends of the handoff should be designed.

lessons.rule: Give a subagent a defined output format, and a description that tells the delegating agent what context to pass.

lessons.explanation: The hook is on the right tool at the right point, but it exits with code 1. In a command hook, only exit code 2 blocks; exit code 1 does not, so the message printed and the command ran anyway. Exiting with code 2 and writing the reason to stderr stops the call and tells Claude why.

a.reasoning: Widening the matcher changes where the check runs, not whether it blocks: every extra check would still exit with code 1 and block nothing.
a.tempting: `Edit` and `Write` can touch config files too, so wider coverage sounds useful.

b.reasoning: CLAUDE.md is guidance Claude usually follows, not enforcement. The hook already exists; only its exit code is wrong.
b.tempting: A written rule tells Claude the reason directly.

c.reasoning: Exit code 2 blocks the call, and stderr becomes the reason Claude sees, so it knows not to try that path again. The script still runs on every `Bash` call, because the matcher selects the tool and the path check is in the script's own code. Only what it does on a match changes, so commands that don't touch `config/prod/` run exactly as they do today. A `permissionDecision` of `deny` would block as well.

d.reasoning: It keeps `exit 1`, which does not block, and a `PostToolUse` hook fires after the command has already run, too late to stop a change to production config.
d.tempting: It keeps the reason the script prints and checks the command that really ran.

concept: `PreToolUse` fires before a tool call and is the enforcement primitive: it can stop the call before it happens. It blocks by returning a `permissionDecision` of `deny`, or by exiting with code 2, with stderr as the reason Claude sees. Exit code 1 does not block; only 2 does.
`PostToolUse` fires after the tool already ran, so blocking there cannot stop the call or its side effects. An instruction in CLAUDE.md is a request that Claude usually follows, not a guarantee.

stemSignals.meaning: The message prints, but exit 1 doesn't block.

stemSignals.meaning: The hook ran and failed to block.

stemSignals.phrase: Other `Bash` commands must keep running without delay
stemSignals.meaning: The fix must not slow or block other commands.

lookFor: The exit code that blocks: 2, with the reason on stderr.
A check that stays before the call.

CLAUDE.md is guidance, and the hook only needs the right exit code.
It keeps `exit 1`, which blocks nothing, and `PostToolUse` runs after the command.

lessons.rule: A command hook blocks only with exit code 2 or a deny decision; exit code 1 reports a problem but lets the call run.

lessons.explanation: The assistant planned all 30 edits from the ticket and applied them in one scripted `sed` pass without inspecting a single class, so it missed the 7 that had already been migrated. An agent has to observe its environment: read before writing, check results, and adjust its approach from what it sees. Here that means reading each class first and building each module after its edits, letting each result reshape the rest of the plan.

a.reasoning: Reading each class catches the 7 hand-migrated ones before they break. Only the modules it touched are built, each once after its own edits, which fits within today, and errors show up one module at a time while the remaining plan can still change. The plan follows the code's real state instead of a list.

b.reasoning: Building at the end checks results, but only after 30 blind edits, so the 7 duplicates and their knock-on errors arrive together across 4 modules. Each result should shape the next step instead.
b.tempting: It does check results, which is half the principle.

c.reasoning: The tracker is a week out of date, so it swaps one stale list for another and still skips reading the code. The classes themselves are the source of truth.
c.tempting: A list of unmigrated classes is exactly what seems to be missing.

d.reasoning: Thirty parallel subagents add 30 contexts and their coordination to a mechanical edit. Nothing in it builds each module or feeds what was found back into the remaining plan, so the 6-minute module builds that catch errors early never shape the work.
d.tempting: Parallel work seems to fit a deadline of today.

concept: An agent must observe its environment, reading before writing and checking results, and adjust its approach from what it sees. In agent designs, the model decides the next step from what it has seen.

The exam guide's Task 1.6 describes adaptive plans that generate subtasks from what each step discovers. A plan written from a list before any file is opened is the opposite: it can't react to what the code actually contains.

Check results after each step, not only at the end.
A plan that changes as results come in.

eliminate.reason: It checks only after 30 blind edits.
It swaps in another stale list and still skips reading.
It adds 30 contexts to a mechanical edit, and no per-module build feeds results back into the plan.

lessons.rule: Let the plan adapt to what each step finds: read before writing, check results as you go, and revise the remaining steps.
